title: Cherry butter dish
subtitle: A two-part butter keeper in seasoned cherry
excerpt: A butter dish in seasoned cherry: a flat base 12 cm by 8 cm, 15 mm thick, and a slab-sided lid 12 cm by 8 cm, 18 mm thick with 10 mm sides. Cherry is the traditional English and American choice for dairy utensils. Plane, scraper, and board-butter finish.

glossaryTerms.definition: Air-dried or kiln-dried wood at a stable moisture content for indoor use (8 to 12 per cent). Does not shrink after working.
A thin steel plate with a turned burr edge used to take very fine shavings from a wood surface, leaving a cleaner finish than sandpaper.
A recessed step cut along the edge of a board to receive a mating piece. In a butter dish, the rebate cut into the underside of the lid sides is what allows the lid to sit over the base.

content.text: A butter dish keeps a half-pound block of butter accessible on the kitchen table without it drying out. The lid sits over the base on a shallow
rebate
cut into its underside; the fit is loose enough to lift without resistance but close enough to exclude most of the air. This project uses
seasoned
cherry, the traditional dairy wood: fine-grained, food-safe, and naturally resistant to staining. Cherry warms to a deep red-brown over years of use.
Wood

Cherry from a PAR board 20 mm thick. Two sections: one 14 cm by 10 cm for the base, and one 14 cm by 10 cm by 20 mm for the lid. Seasoned cherry turns from pale tan to a warm amber-red over two to three years; the initial pale colour should not be mistaken for a poor-quality piece. Maple or pear are the alternatives: both are fine-grained and food-safe.
Method
Step 1: Plane the base
The base is a flat slab 12 cm by 8 cm, 15 mm thick. Plane the top face to a flat surface with the smoothing plane. Use the
card scraper
to finish the surface. Chamfer the underside edges with the block plane: 2 mm chamfer all around so the base sits comfortably on a flat surface without rocking.
Step 2: Prepare the lid blank
The lid starts as a 14 cm by 10 cm by 20 mm block. The lid body will be 18 mm thick when finished; the extra 2 mm is worked off in planing. Plane all faces flat.
Step 3: Cut the rebate

Mark the rebate on all four edges of the lid underside: 10 mm wide and 10 mm deep. The rebate removes a frame of material from the underside, leaving a central platform that the butter sits on and a skirt of 10 mm sides that drops over the base. Cut the rebate shoulders first with a bench chisel and mallet to define the rebate depth, then pare the cheeks back to the 10 mm width. Check the fit against the base after each pass.
Step 4: Plane and scrape the lid top
Plane the lid top surface flat. Apply a slight dome (2 mm crown at the centre) if preferred; this traditional form sheds any condensation that might form on the lid surface. Scrape to a fine finish.
Finishing

Apply board butter (a mixture of beeswax and food-safe oil) to all surfaces of both pieces. Rub in with a cloth, leave ten minutes, buff off. Board butter is immediately food-safe with no cure time. It is softer than danish oil and needs reapplication every few weeks on a piece in daily use, but it is the most appropriate finish for a food-contact dairy piece. The butter dish can be used the same day.

attrs.symptom: The lid rebate is too tight and the lid does not seat
attrs.cause: The rebate was cut 0.5 mm undersize on one or both dimensions.
attrs.fix: Pare the rebate walls back by a further half-millimetre on the tight sides. Test the fit repeatedly: once the fit is correct (it should drop on without force), stop.

attrs.symptom: The cherry surface has tear-out marks from the plane
attrs.cause: The plane iron was cutting against the grain direction in cherry's wavy figure.
attrs.fix: Reverse the plane direction on the affected area. Cherry requires careful grain reading; the card scraper is more reliable than the plane for final finishing.
